why: The statement quantifies over every locally compact group and every topological manifold. Both 2026 claims (OpenAI, and Dabrowski) prove the Lie conclusion only for second-countable Hausdorff groups on connected, second-countable, boundaryless manifolds, so I scored them as case, not whole. This was the close call. Second countability of the manifold is often built into the definition of 'manifold', and the reduction to the Z_p statement is standard, so a whole reading is defensible. I decided against it because formal-conjectures issue #6914 explicitly says the group reduction 'needs an argument', and the paper itself does not treat the excluded cases. Both 2026 claims are unreviewed: the Lean build covers a weaker C∞ variant, and a clean build is not digestion. I rated them doubtful rather than not_credible. The method is serious and there has been only about a week for expert reaction. The only technical objection is an opaque AI audit, which can neither knock a claim down nor clear it. On AI role: for OpenAI I scored generated, resting on the repository-wide statement that the manuscripts were produced by the internal model, with no exception listed for this paper. For Dabrowski I also scored generated, because the author line itself credits the AI agents as the authors; that basis is thin. The OpenAI release appears as two events (openai-2026-hs-preprint and openai-math-304) that are the same manuscript, so both rows carry the same answers. Shelukhin (2024) restricts the class of actions to symplectic or Hamiltonian ones, which makes it a case, just as the Lipschitz and Hölder results are. McAuley's 2001 full claim meets several F10 signals at once, so I scored it not_credible.
doubts: openai-2026-hs-preprint and openai-math-304 are duplicate entries for one manuscript. Its date is taken as the public release (6 Oct 2026); either date is after the snapshot. The AI attribution for the OpenAI paper rests on a repository-wide README sentence, not on the paper's own text. The 'whole' versus 'case' call on the second-countability and connectedness hypotheses depends on whether the reduction to second-countable groups is routine, which the record does not settle. The pre-window journal events (Bochner–Montgomery, Malešič and others) are known from search summaries only.
